Summer Projects Should Be Student-Designed

Every June, students walk out of school with a long stretch of unstructured time and, in many districts, a packet of assignments to keep their minds from going soft. The goal is sound. Research on the "summer slide" shows that students can lose a meaningful portion of their math and reading skills over the break. But the question of who should design the work matters a great deal. Summer projects should be student-designed, with teachers acting as guides, because ownership produces effort, authentic learning, and skills that a worksheet never could.

The strongest argument for student design is motivation. A teacher-designed project arrives in the middle of summer as one more obligation, and students treat it that way. They put it off until August, copy answers from a friend, or rush through it the night before school starts. Nothing about the task belongs to them. When students pick their own topics, the dynamic reverses. A student who loves basketball might spend the summer analyzing shooting percentages and building a statistical model that predicts which players improve most. That same student, handed a generic packet of probability problems, would likely produce the minimum. Interest is a renewable resource, and student-designed projects tap it directly.

A second reason is that designing a project is itself an education. Teacher-designed assignments hide the hardest part of real work, which is deciding what to do. Someone has already chosen the question, the format, and the deadline. A student who must write a proposal has to narrow a vague curiosity into a manageable question, estimate how long each stage will take, and plan around the problems that will come up. These are the habits that college professors and employers say young people lack. A girl who decides to build a small vegetable garden and document its growth must learn to budget, research soil conditions, record observations, and adjust when the tomatoes fail. She learns science, but she also learns to manage her own time, and no packet teaches that.

Critics respond that students left alone will choose easy projects or none at all. This is a fair worry, but it argues for structure rather than for teacher control. Schools can require a short proposal in June that the teacher reviews and approves, with a few check-in points over the summer and a presentation in the fall. The teacher sets the standard, perhaps requiring research, a written reflection, and some evidence of sustained effort, while the student chooses the subject. A teacher can push a weak proposal toward something more ambitious. A student who wants to "watch documentaries" might be asked to compare how three films treat the same historical event and write about the differences. The teacher's expertise raises the quality of the work without taking the work away.

Another objection is fairness. Teacher-designed projects give every student the same assignment, which makes grading simple and equal. But sameness is not the same as fairness. Students come back from summer with very different resources. One may have a library card and a quiet house, while another works a part-time job and watches younger siblings. A rigid assignment that assumes access to museums, travel, or a computer favors the advantaged. A flexible student-designed project lets each person build something that fits their circumstances. The working student might interview coworkers about their jobs and write an essay on the local economy, which requires only a notebook and curiosity.

Finally, consider what students remember. Few people recall a worksheet from the summer after sixth grade. Many recall the time they built a birdhouse, wrote a short story, or taught themselves to code a simple game. Those experiences stick because the person made them. A student who finishes a self-chosen project returns to school with something to show and the confidence that comes from having shaped it.

Summer learning matters, and schools are right to protect it. The best way to do that is to trust students to design the work, hold them accountable through proposals and presentations, and let teachers coach rather than command. When learning belongs to the student, it lasts well beyond September.
